structure:
Part 11, animals visual and security suites. Read in full: the 12 visual-regression specs under tests/animals/e2e/visual (origin-of-import, import-reason, arrival-details, transited-countries, identification-card, upload-documents, party-picker, date-picker, overview-totals, review, refused-review, declaration) and the names of the 46 committed PNG baselines beside them in *-snapshots folders (listed with find, never read as pixels); the 8 frontend security specs under tests/animals/security (frontend-auth, frontend-notification-journey, frontend-conditional-pages, frontend-lifecycle, frontend-documents, frontend-draft-validation-error, frontend-dashboard-params, frontend-trail); the fixtures the two suites use (fixtures/visual.ts, fixtures/security.ts); utils/frozen-date-picker.ts; all four files of utils/zap (client.ts, prime-context.ts, check-context-sync.ts, run-and-gate.ts); config/zap.ts; the three ZAP Automation Framework plans (zap/automation-passive.yaml, zap/automation-active.yaml, zap/automation-context.yaml) and zap/rules.tsv; docs/security.md; and bin/update-visual-baselines-linux.sh. Read as supporting context, not claimed except where a spec rests on them: page-objects/shared/date-picker.ts, page-objects/shared/address-picker-results.ts, page-objects/shared/base-page.ts (journeyStrip, TRAIL_START), page-objects/shared/sets.ts, page-objects/animals/party-picker-page.ts, utils/playwright/shared-config.ts (the 1280x1000 project viewport), utils/playwright/legacy-scrollers-browser.ts and package.json's security scripts.

The slice holds 23 visual test declarations across the 12 visual specs (2+5+1+2+1+1+1+5+1+1+2+1) and 9 test declarations across the 8 frontend security specs (frontend-lifecycle holds two, the other seven one each). Both are smaller than the partition's own counts of 60 and 26; the files are the evidence and the counts are recorded as they are. Covered: every visual test by title with the page or component it photographs, its baseline file names, its viewport, and what is masked, pinned or frozen to make the shot stable; every baseline file name, each present for both chromium-darwin and chromium-linux; every frontend security test by title with the journey it walks for the scan; the ZAP set-up as rules (six contexts, their excluded diagnostic paths, their dataDrivenNodes, the three-plan sync rule, the DOM-XSS rule turned off, the 60-minute cap, the alert-rating gate, the truncation gate and the no-traffic gate); the scan profiles and the three lanes that run them; which services are deliberately not scanned and why; and the coverage gaps the suites and docs/security.md leave open. The backend security spec under tests/animals/security/backend is part 9's and is not claimed here.

claims.statement: The animals visual-regression suite is a separate, tagged suite: every one of its 12 specs declares the tag @visual on its describe block, so it is selected and excluded by that tag rather than by folder.
claims.ref: tests/animals/e2e/visual/*.visual.spec.ts, each describe block
claims.quote: test.describe('Origin of import (visual regression)', { tag: '@visual' }, () => {

claims.statement: Every visual spec forces a headless browser for itself rather than relying on the run's default, so a headed debugging run cannot quietly produce different pixels.
claims.ref: tests/animals/e2e/visual/origin-of-import.visual.spec.ts:4 (and the same line in all 12 visual specs)
claims.quote: test.use({ headless: true });

claims.quote: review-desktop-chromium-darwin.png
claims.note: Counted with find over the -snapshots folders; the PNGs themselves were not read.

claims.statement: On macOS the visual suite photographs the page in a browser launched with always-shown scroll bars and a coarse pointer, whatever the developer's own mouse and scroll-bar settings, so a Mac shot matches the Linux baseline.
claims.ref: fixtures/visual.ts:8-19 with utils/playwright/legacy-scrollers-browser.ts:54-69
claims.quote: export const test = process.platform === 'darwin' ? legacyScrollersTest : base;
claims.note: mechanism: swaps the worker's browser for a headless shell started with -AppleShowScrollBars Always and --blink-settings=primaryHoverType=2,availableHoverTypes=2,primaryPointerType=4,availablePointerTypes=4, so the shot's scroll bars and hover styling do not depend on the host.

claims.statement: Every full-page visual shot of a journey page hides the journey strip, the band that carries the notification's own reference number and status tag, so a fresh reference number each run does not break the comparison.
claims.ref: tests/animals/e2e/visual/origin-of-import.visual.spec.ts:13-14 with page-objects/shared/base-page.ts:142-152
claims.quote: mask: [animalsPages.originOfImport.journeyStrip],
claims.note: mechanism: the journey strip locator is '.app-journey-strip', which holds the status tag and the notification reference.

claims.statement: Visual shots are taken at a 1280 by 1000 viewport unless a test changes it, that being the width and height every Playwright project in the suite sets.
claims.ref: utils/playwright/shared-config.ts:26
claims.quote: const viewport = { width: 1280, height: 1000 };
claims.note: Inferred because no visual spec states its own viewport except refused-review's phone test; the figure comes from the shared Playwright config, whose own claims belong to the configuration part.

claims.statement: A visual shot of a page that shows a date replaces the date's text with 1 November 2026 before the shot, so a page whose content moves with today's date still has a fixed baseline.
claims.ref: fixtures/visual.ts:27-29
claims.note: mechanism: writes textContent into the located element in the browser.

claims.statement: A visual shot of a notification's view header replaces the reference number with GBN-AG-26-AAAAAA in both places it appears and the created date with "Date created: 1 January 2026".
claims.ref: fixtures/visual.ts:31-35
claims.note: The header shows the reference number twice, as a heading-level reference and as a named value.

claims.statement: A visual shot of a date picker can be taken as though today were a fixed day: the browser clock stops at noon on that day and every picker's earliest and latest allowed dates move by the same number of days before the picker reads them, so the calendar's greyed-out days stay put.
claims.ref: utils/frozen-date-picker.ts:32-45
claims.quote:
Makes every date picker the page loads behave as though today were `today`
 * (a `yyyy-mm-dd` civil date): the browser clock stops at noon that day and
 * each picker's served `data-min-date` and `data-max-date` move by the same
 * number of days before the picker reads them. Call it before the page loads.
claims.note: mechanism: shifts the data-min-date and data-max-date attributes on every element that carries them, on readystatechange at document.readyState 'interactive', and sets a fixed clock.

claims.statement: Linux visual baselines are regenerated from a Mac by running the @visual suite in a Playwright Linux container against the local workspace stack, one worker at a time, with the repo bind-mounted so the updated PNGs land on the host owned by the person who ran it.

claims.quote: run _test_docker_compose -- --grep @visual --update-snapshots --workers=1 "$@"

claims.statement: The security scan is dynamic application security testing with OWASP ZAP as a proxy: Playwright drives real signed-in journeys through it instead of letting ZAP crawl, so ZAP attacks what a real session touched.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, opening paragraph
claims.quote: A DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) scan using [OWASP ZAP](https://www.zaproxy.org/) as a proxy. Playwright drives real authenticated journeys through it rather than letting ZAP crawl, so it observes what a real session touches and then attacks that.

claims.statement: Scan coverage is traffic-driven, so any route no spec drives is invisible to the scan; the attacking corpus is therefore curated by hand rather than generated.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, 'Coverage is therefore traffic-driven'
claims.quote: Coverage is therefore **traffic-driven**: a route no spec drives is invisible to the scan. That is why the `@active` corpus is curated by hand rather than generated.
claims.note: Stated in general terms: the weakness is one of coverage, not of any particular route.

claims.statement: There are two security profiles: a passive one that runs the end-to-end suite without the attacking specs and does not attack, and an attacking one that runs only the attacking specs and is deliberate and docker-compose only.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, Profiles table
claims.quote:
| `security`        | The e2e suite, excluding `@active` | No — passive only | Cheap, run broadly              |
| `security:active` | The `@active` suite only           | Yes               | Deliberate; docker-compose only |

claims.statement: The attacking specs are kept out of the passive profile because they walk the same journeys a second time and include destructive steps.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, note under the Profiles table
claims.quote: `@active` is excluded from the passive profile because it walks the same journeys a second time and includes destructive steps.

claims.statement: The attacking profile is refused on the CDP platform: the attacking specs delete notifications, documents and dead-letter messages and the scan refires each with fuzzed payloads, which is acceptable against a throwaway stack and destructive against a shared one, so the entrypoint fails the run instead.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, '`security:active` is refused on CDP'
claims.quote: The `@active` suite deletes notifications, documents and DLQ messages, and the active scan re-fires each with fuzzed payloads — fine against a disposable stack, destructive against a shared one. `entrypoint.sh` writes to `FAILED` rather than running it.

claims.statement: Guarding only the production environment is not enough to keep the attacking profile off shared environments, because such a guard would still have let dev, test and perf-test run it.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, same paragraph
claims.quote: The `throwIfProdEnvironment` guard is no help here: it stops `prod` alone, so `dev`, `test` and `perf-test` would all have run.

claims.statement: The scan runs in three lanes that do not share a configuration or a target: locally against the localhost stack in either profile, from a GitHub Action against a stack on the runner in the attacking profile, and on the CDP portal against a deployed environment in the passive profile only.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, 'How it runs' table
claims.quote: | **CDP portal**    | `PROFILE` env var → `entrypoint.sh`                                                                         | `playwright.config.ts`                | deployed `${ENVIRONMENT}` | `security` or `<domain>:security` only  |

claims.statement: The GitHub Action that runs the attacking scan is manual dispatch only and its nightly schedule stays switched off until an end-to-end run has been verified.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, paragraph after the lanes table
claims.quote: The GitHub Action is manual dispatch only; the nightly schedule stays disabled pending a verified end-to-end run.

claims.statement: The attacking scan's report is published to a public GitHub Pages site under a dated path and is password-protected for that reason, and reports older than seven days are deleted.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, same paragraph
claims.quote: Its report publishes to GitHub Pages under `security-active/<date>/`, password-protected via the `ZAP_REPORT_PASSWORD` secret because that Pages site is otherwise public. Reports older than 7 days are pruned.
claims.note: The password itself is a repository secret and is not in the source; nothing here names a value.

claims.statement: Six services are in the scan, each as its own named ZAP context: the animals frontend, the animals admin, the INS frontend, the animals backend, the plants backend and the address book.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, 'What gets scanned' table, and zap/automation-context.yaml env.contexts
claims.quote:
| `trade-imports-animals-frontend` | 3000       | `frontend`        |
| `trade-imports-animals-admin`    | 3001       | `admin`           |
| `trade-imports-ins-frontend`     | 3002       | `ins`             |
| `trade-imports-animals-backend`  | 8085       | `animals-backend` |
| `trade-imports-plants-backend`   | 8091       | `plants-backend`  |
| `trade-imports-address-book`     | 8089       | `address-book`    |

claims.statement: Each context's address is supplied by its own environment variable rather than hard-coded, so the same plans point at the compose stack's ports locally and at a per-service subdomain on CDP.
claims.ref: zap/automation-context.yaml env.contexts urls; docs/security.md, 'Ports are the compose stack's'
claims.quote: Ports are the compose stack's; on CDP each service is a per-service subdomain.

claims.statement: Diagnostic endpoints are left out of every context rather than scanned: health and static assets on the three Node apps, and health, info, metrics, cache and env on the three Java services.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, 'Diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned'; zap/automation-context.yaml excludePaths for every context
claims.quote: Diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned: `/health` and static assets on the Node contexts, and the full actuator set (`/health`, `/info`, `/metrics`, `/cache`, `/env`) on the three Java services.
claims.note: The Java services' diagnostic endpoints sit on the API's own root namespace, not under a prefix, because the actuator base path is "/" in each service's own configuration.

claims.statement: The identifiers in a page or API address are declared to ZAP as data rather than structure, so each run's notification does not appear as a brand-new branch of the site tree and the identifier itself becomes something the scan can attack: the notification id and upload id on the animals frontend, the address id on the INS frontend, the reference number and upload id on the animals backend, the reference number on the plants backend, and the organisation id and address id on the address book.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml env.contexts structure.dataDrivenNodes (every context), with the frontend comment at lines 15-21
claims.quote:
dataDrivenNodes tells ZAP the segment
    # is data, not structure: one folded node, and the id becomes an
    # injection point (IDOR-style access-by-id checks included).
claims.note: This is how the suite tests for access to another organisation's record by guessing its identifier.

claims.statement: Those structure rules only apply to parts of the site tree as they are first seen, so the contexts are registered on ZAP by a plan of their own before any journey runs; registering them with the scanning plan afterwards would be too late for the identifiers to be recognised as data.
claims.ref: zap/automation-context.yaml, header comment; utils/zap/prime-context.ts
claims.quote:
Structural Modifiers (dataDrivenNodes) and excludePaths only apply to
# site-tree nodes as they're *added* — they don't retroactively reshape
# nodes that already exist.

claims.statement: The context-registration plan declares one do-nothing job only because a plan must have at least one, there being no traffic yet to wait for.
claims.ref: zap/automation-context.yaml, jobs
claims.quote:
# No traffic exists yet at this point in the run, so there's nothing to
  # wait for — this job only exists because a plan needs at least one job.

claims.statement: All three ZAP plans must declare exactly the same contexts, and a run stops with an explanatory error before registering anything if they have drifted apart, because ZAP offers no way to share that block between plans.
claims.ref: utils/zap/check-context-sync.ts:38-58, called from utils/zap/prime-context.ts
claims.quote: `env.contexts in ${mismatches.join(', ')} doesn't match ${BASELINE_FILE} — ZAP has no way to share this block across plans, so all three must be kept identical.`

claims.statement: The attacking plan runs one attack job per context, six in all, each capped at 60 minutes.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml, the six activeScan jobs
claims.quote:
- type: activeScan
    parameters:
      context: frontend
      ... 
      maxScanDurationInMins: 60
claims.note: Quote abbreviated across the job's comment block; the same two parameters appear on each of the six jobs.

claims.statement: The 60-minute cap is a runaway guard rather than a budget, set at about four and a half times the slowest context measured: the animals frontend took 13 minutes 27 seconds, the admin 4 minutes 39, the INS frontend 1 minute 25, the backend 1 minute 17 and the address book 21 seconds, 21 minutes in all.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml, frontend activeScan comment
claims.quote:
A runaway guard, not a budget. Measured: frontend 13m27s, admin 4m39s,
      # ins 1m25s, backend 1m17s, address-book 21s — 21m total, frontend 64% of
